unit.unitOverview: This unit is about the studying itself. It gives you the language to say what you can and cannot do yet, to read the instruction at the top of an exercise and know what it is asking, and — most useful of all — to stop a conversation politely when you have not understood. That last one is not a small skill. Learners who can say sorry, can you say that again more slowly get far more practice than learners who nod and hope.
unit.learningPath:

Open Patterns. Card 3 is the one to study hardest — it is how you read every instruction from here on.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a course timetable.
Do the Practice. Try each exercise before you open its answer.
Record yourself asking for help four different ways.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about studying, which means it is about the words you need in order to keep learning after this course ends.
Four patterns.
The first is can and cannot. This is how English says what you are able to do. I can read English. I cannot speak it well yet. She can understand but she cannot write.
Three things make can easy. It never changes: I can, she can, we can — never she cans. There is no do in the question: you say Can you help me, not Do you can help me. And the verb after it has no to: I can read, never I can to read.
The short form of cannot is can't. In speech, can and can't sound very similar, and in fast speech the difference is mostly the vowel. If you are not sure whether someone said can or can't, ask. That is what pattern four is for.
Second pattern: the s on the end of the verb. This one is small and it is everywhere.
In the present, English adds s to the verb — but only for he, she and it. I like. You like. We like. They like. But: he likes, she likes, it likes.
One letter, one place, and it is the most common written error in beginner English. Not because it is difficult, but because it carries no meaning. If you say she like English, everybody understands you perfectly. Nothing is lost. So there is no pressure from the conversation to fix it, and it survives for years. You have to fix it deliberately.
The same s goes on every verb in the present, not only like. He works. She reads. It costs.
Third pattern, and this is the one I want you to study hardest: the words that instructions use.
Every exercise you meet from now on begins with a command. Write. Choose. Match. Complete. Underline. Circle. Tick. Answer. Put in order. Look up.
These words are not conversation. You will almost never say them. But if you cannot read them, you cannot do the exercise, and you will lose time not because the English was hard but because you did not know what was being asked. Ten of these words unlock every workbook, every online exercise, and every test you will take.
Notice they all have the same shape: the plain verb, with no I, no you, nobody in front of it. That shape is how English gives an instruction.
Fourth pattern: asking for help. And I want to be direct about why this matters.
When you do not understand, you have two choices. You can nod, and say nothing, and hope. Or you can say: sorry, can you repeat that? Can you say it more slowly? What does that word mean? How do you spell it?
Learners who ask get the sentence again, slower, and often in easier words. They learn from the repair. Learners who nod get nothing, and the conversation moves on without them.
So learn these four phrases properly, until they come out without thinking:
Sorry, can you repeat that?
Can you speak more slowly, please?
What does ... mean?
How do you spell it?
Nobody minds. Nobody has ever minded. Asking is not a sign that your English is bad — it is what people do in their own language too.
Go to Patterns and work through the four cards.

readings.title: Twenty Minutes, Every Day
readings.passageScript:
Here is something worth knowing early.
Twenty minutes every day is better than three hours once a week. This is not an opinion. It is how memory works.
When you study for three hours, you forget most of it before you come back. When you study for twenty minutes and come back tomorrow, you meet the same words again while they are still there, and each time they stay a little longer.
So the question is not how many hours have I got. The question is where are my twenty minutes.
On the bus. Before the others wake up. While the water boils. In the ten minutes you are waiting for something.
Two more things.
Say it out loud. Reading silently feels like studying, and it is — but only for reading. If you never move your mouth, your mouth never learns. You can say a sentence quietly, under your breath, in a room with other people, and nobody will notice.
And write down the words you meet, not the words you are given. A word you needed today and could not find is worth ten words from a list. Write it in a notebook. Look at the notebook on the bus.

readings.title: What To Say When You Do Not Understand
readings.passageScript:
This is the most useful page in the unit.
When you do not understand, you have two choices. Nod and hope, or ask.
If you nod, the conversation moves on and you have learned nothing. If you ask, the person says it again — usually more slowly, often in easier words — and you learn from the repair. Learners who ask improve faster. That is the whole reason this page exists.
Here are four things to say. Learn them until they come out without thinking.
Sorry, can you repeat that? — Use this when you heard nothing, or nearly nothing.
Can you speak more slowly, please? — Use this when you heard the words but they came too fast to hold.
What does ... mean? — Use this for one word. Put the word in the gap: What does deposit mean?
How do you spell it? — Use this when you have heard a word and want to write it down or look it up.
A fifth, for when you have understood some of it: Sorry, I understood the first part but not the end.
That one is worth learning too, because it tells the person exactly where to start again. It saves you both time.
One last thing, and it is the important one. Nobody minds. People ask each other to repeat things in their own language every day. Asking is not a sign that your English is bad. It is a sign that you are still in the conversation.

grammar.title: Can and cannot
grammar.explanation: This is how English says what you are able to do. It is one of the easiest patterns in the language because the word never changes, and it is one of the most useful because you need it to describe your own English.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I can read.        I cannot read.
You can read.      You cannot read.
He can read.       He cannot read.
She can read.      She cannot read.
We can read.       We cannot read.
They can read.     They cannot read.

Question: Can you help me?  Can she come?
Short form: can't

Never: she cans · do you can · I can to read
grammar.workedExample:
Make a question from: She can come on Saturday.
1. Find can.
2. Move it to the front: Can she…
3. Leave the rest exactly as it was: come on Saturday.
4. Change the full stop to a question mark.
Result: Can she come on Saturday?
Notice what you did NOT add. No do. No to. English questions with can need neither, and adding either is the usual mistake.
grammar.commonMistake: Three errors, all easy to avoid. Adding s — she cans. Adding do — do you can help me. Adding to — I can to read. Can needs none of them: the word never changes, and the verb after it is plain.
grammar.memoryTip: Can never changes and never takes to.
grammar.practice:
Write the sentence correctly.
1. She can to speak three languages.
2. Do you can help me?
3. He cans read but he cannot write.
4. I can to come on Monday.
5. Can she to repeat that?
grammar.answerKey:
1. She can speak three languages. (no to)
2. Can you help me? (no do — just move can to the front)
3. He can read but he cannot write. (no s on can)
4. I can come on Monday. (no to)
5. Can she repeat that? (no to)

grammar.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
grammar.title: The s that only he, she and it take
grammar.explanation: In the present tense English adds s to the verb — but only for he, she and it. This is the most common written error in beginner English, and not because it is difficult. It carries no meaning, so nothing in the conversation forces you to fix it. You have to fix it deliberately.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I like        We like
You like      They like
He likes
She likes
It likes

Same for every verb:
he works · she reads · it costs · he practises

With do and does:
I do not like.  He does not like.
Do you like?    Does he like?
grammar.workedExample:
Write the correct form: She ____ (practise) every day.
1. Who is the sentence about? She.
2. Is that he, she or it? Yes — she.
3. So the verb takes s.
4. Add it: practises.
Result: She practises every day.
Now the same verb with a different subject: They practise every day. No s, because they is not he, she or it. The verb did not change for any other reason.
grammar.commonMistake: Leaving the s off — she like English. Everybody will understand you perfectly, which is exactly the problem: the conversation gives you no reason to correct it. The opposite error also happens once learners notice the rule — they like becomes they likes. The s belongs to three subjects only.
grammar.memoryTip: He, she, it — add the s. Everything else, leave it alone.
grammar.practice:
Write the correct form of the verb.
1. She ____ (read) the news every morning.
2. They ____ (work) at the weekend.
3. He ____ (practise) on the bus.
4. I ____ (like) the speaking exercises.
5. My teacher ____ (speak) very quickly.
6. We ____ (study) together.
Then make numbers 1 and 4 negative.
grammar.answerKey:
1. reads  2. work  3. practises  4. like  5. speaks  6. study
Negatives: She does not read the news every morning. I do not like the speaking exercises.
Number 5 is the one to check — my teacher is one person, so it behaves exactly like he or she and takes the s. Watch the negatives too: once you use does, the s moves onto does and comes off the main verb.

grammar.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
grammar.title: The words instructions use
grammar.explanation: Every exercise you will ever meet begins with one of about ten words. You will almost never say them, but if you cannot read them you cannot do the exercise — and you will lose time not because the English was hard but because you did not know what was being asked.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Write    put words on the page
Choose   pick one from several
Match    join two lists together
Complete fill in what is missing
Underline draw a line under a word
Circle   draw a ring around it
Tick     put a ✓ next to it
Answer   respond to a question
Put in order  rearrange them
Look up  find it in a dictionary

All of them are the plain verb with nobody in front.
grammar.workedExample:
Read this instruction: Complete the sentences with the correct form of the verb.
1. Find the instruction word: Complete.
2. Complete means fill in what is missing.
3. What is missing? The sentences have gaps.
4. What goes in them? The correct form of the verb.
So: there are gaps, and you write a verb in each one, in the right form.
You now know what to do without anybody explaining it. That is the whole skill — and you will use it in every book and every test from here on.
grammar.commonMistake: The commonest problem is not misreading the word but skipping it — starting the exercise from the first item and working out the task from the shape of the questions. That works until an exercise looks familiar and is not, and then you do the wrong thing carefully. Read the instruction first, every time.
grammar.memoryTip: Read the instruction before the first question. Always.
grammar.practice:
What does each instruction ask you to do? Answer in your own words.
1. Underline the verb in each sentence.
2. Match the word to its meaning.
3. Put the sentences in order.
4. Complete the table.
5. Tick the correct answer.
6. Look up the words you do not know.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Draw a line under the verb — one word in each sentence.
2. Join each word in one list to the right meaning in the other list.
3. Rearrange them so they are in the right sequence.
4. Fill in the empty boxes in the table.
5. Put a ✓ next to the right one — not a circle, not a line.
6. Find them in a dictionary.
If you were unsure about any of these, write it in your notebook. You will meet all six many times.

grammar.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
grammar.title: Asking someone to repeat or slow down
grammar.explanation: This is the most useful pattern in the unit and possibly in the level. Learners who ask get the sentence again, slower and often in easier words, and learn from the repair. Learners who nod get nothing.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Sorry, can you repeat that?
   — you heard nothing

Can you speak more slowly, please?
   — you heard it, but too fast

What does ____ mean?
   — one word you do not know

How do you spell it?
   — you want to write it down

Sorry, I understood the first part but not the end.
   — you got some of it
grammar.workedExample:
Someone says a long sentence and you catch the beginning only.
1. Ask: did I hear nothing, or something? Something.
2. So do not ask for the whole thing again — that wastes both your time.
3. Say where you stopped: Sorry, I understood the first part but not the end.
4. The other person starts again from the middle, not the beginning.
That is the difference between a good repair and a slow one. Naming where you stopped is more useful than asking for everything again.
grammar.commonMistake: The real error is not a wrong phrase — it is saying nothing. Nodding when you have not understood feels polite and costs you the sentence. Asking costs three seconds. There is also one wrong form worth fixing: it is What does this word mean, never What means this word.
grammar.memoryTip: Three seconds of asking beats a whole sentence lost.
grammar.practice:
Which phrase would you use?
1. The person spoke and you caught nothing at all.
2. You heard every word but it was too fast to follow.
3. You know all the words except one.
4. You have heard a word and you want to write it in your notebook.
5. You followed the beginning and lost the end.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Sorry, can you repeat that?
2. Can you speak more slowly, please?
3. What does ____ mean?
4. How do you spell it?
5. Sorry, I understood the first part but not the end.
Say all five out loud twice now. These are worth knowing by heart, because you need them at the moment when thinking is hardest.

writing.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
writing.title: Writing 1 — Six people, six verbs
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write twelve sentences in the present tense.
Six about yourself or other people (I, you, we, they) — no s on the verb.
Six about one person or one thing (he, she, it) — s on the verb.
Underline every verb.
Then count: exactly six of your underlined verbs should end in s.
writing.modelText:
1. I practise for twenty minutes every day.
2. We study on Wednesday evenings.
3. They work at the weekend.
4. You speak very clearly.
5. I read the news in English.
6. My friends come to the Saturday class.
7. She practises on the bus.
8. He works at the weekend.
9. My teacher speaks very quickly.
10. She reads the news every morning.
11. It costs nothing.
12. My neighbour studies at home.
writing.successCriteria: Twelve sentences; every verb underlined; exactly six end in s; the six with s all have he, she, it or one named person as the subject; no verb has s for I, you, we or they
writing.support: Write the six without s first — they are easier. Then write the six with s and check each subject is genuinely one person or one thing before you add the letter.
writing.extension: Rewrite four of the sentences as negatives, and notice what happens to the s when does appears.

writing.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
writing.title: Writing 2 — What you can and cannot do yet
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write eight sentences about your English.
Four with can, four with cannot.
Add yet to at least three of the cannot sentences.
Then add one more sentence at the end saying which of the four cannot sentences you want to change first, and why that one.
writing.modelText:
I can read simple texts.
I can understand numbers and dates.
I can ask someone to repeat something.
I can fill in a form with my own details.
I cannot speak on the telephone yet.
I cannot follow two people talking to each other yet.
I cannot write a formal letter.
I cannot understand the news on the radio yet.
I want to change the telephone one first, because I need it to make appointments and I avoid calling anybody.
writing.successCriteria: Four can and four cannot sentences; yet used at least three times; no to after can; the final sentence names one specific thing and gives a real reason
writing.support: Do not start with the cannot list — it is discouraging and harder. Write the four can sentences first. You will find there are more than four.
writing.extension: Keep this page. Write the date on it, and answer the same eight questions again at the end of the level.

writing.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
writing.title: Writing 3 — Where are your twenty minutes?
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Reading 1 says the question is not how many hours you have, but where your twenty minutes are.
Write a study plan for one week.
For each of the seven days, write the time, the place, and the one thing you will do.
Be specific. On the bus at 07:40 — read my notebook is a plan. Study more is not.
Then write two sentences: which day will be hardest, and what you will do instead if that day fails.
writing.modelText:
Monday — 07:40, on the bus — read the new words in my notebook
Tuesday — 21:00, kitchen — Patterns cards 1 and 2
Wednesday — 07:40, on the bus — say the four help phrases out loud
Thursday — 13:00, at work, break — read one page
Friday — 21:00, kitchen — the writing exercise
Saturday — 10:00, at home — the whole unit quiz
Sunday — 09:00, at home — record myself and listen back
Thursday will be hardest because my break is often cancelled. If it fails I will do ten minutes on the bus home instead.
writing.successCriteria: Seven days, each with a time, a place and one specific task; no vague entries; the two final sentences name a real day and a real alternative
writing.support: Start from your week as it already is, not from the study. Find the gaps that already exist — waiting, travelling, before others are awake — and put the study into them. A plan that needs new time usually fails.
writing.extension: At the end of the week, tick the days you actually did and write one sentence about what that tells you.

writing.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Every sentence below has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each one out correctly, and say which pattern it came from.
1. She can to speak four languages.
2. He like the speaking exercises.
3. Do you can help me?
4. They likes studying in the morning.
5. What means this word?
6. My teacher speak very quickly.
7. She cans read but she cannot write.
8. I can to come on Saturday.
writing.modelText:
1. She can speak four languages. (Pattern 1 — no to after can)
2. He likes the speaking exercises. (Pattern 2 — he takes the s)
3. Can you help me? (Pattern 1 — no do; move can to the front)
4. They like studying in the morning. (Pattern 2 — they does not take the s)
5. What does this word mean? (Pattern 4 — the question is What does … mean)
6. My teacher speaks very quickly. (Pattern 2 — one person, so the s goes on)
7. She can read but she cannot write. (Pattern 1 — can never takes s)
8. I can come on Saturday. (Pattern 1 — no to after can)
writing.successCriteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; no new mistakes introduced
writing.support: Sort them into two piles first: the ones about can and the ones about the s. Six of the eight fall into one of those two piles, and once sorted the fix is obvious.
writing.extension: Look back at anything you wrote earlier in this unit and check every verb that follows he, she or it.

activities.instructionsAndItems:
Some of these are correct and some have one mistake. Write C for correct, or write the sentence properly.
1. I can read simple texts.
2. She can to write very well.
3. Can you repeat that, please?
4. He cans understand but he cannot speak.

6. They cannot follow the news yet.
7. Can she to help me?

1. C  2. She can write very well.  3. C  4. He can understand but he cannot speak.  5. Can you come on Monday?  6. C  7. Can she help me?  8. C  9. I cannot remember the word.  10. C

activities.title: Practice 2 — Add the s, or do not
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write the correct present-tense form of the verb in brackets.
1. She ____ (read) the news every morning.
2. They ____ (work) at the weekend.
3. My teacher ____ (speak) very quickly.
4. I ____ (practise) on the bus.
5. He ____ (study) at home.
6. We ____ (come) on Wednesdays.
7. It ____ (cost) nothing.
8. My neighbour ____ (like) the Saturday class.
9. You ____ (speak) very clearly.
10. The students ____ (write) in their notebooks.
11. She ____ (not like) tests.
12. Do they ____ (understand) the question?
activities.answerSummary:
1. reads  2. work  3. speaks  4. practise  5. studies  6. come  7. costs  8. likes  9. speak  10. write  11. does not like  12. understand
Four to look at. Number 3 and number 8 — my teacher and my neighbour are each one person, so they behave exactly like he or she. Number 5 — study becomes studies, because the y changes to ies. Numbers 11 and 12 — once does or do appears, the s moves onto it and comes off the main verb.
Ten or more correct means this is working. Below ten, redo the Pattern 2 card first.

activities.title: Practice 3 — What is the instruction asking?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Match each instruction to what it asks you to do.
Instructions:
a) Underline the verb.
b) Match the word to its meaning.
c) Complete the sentence.
d) Tick the correct answer.
e) Put the words in order.
f) Circle the odd one out.
g) Look up the word.

What it asks:
1. Fill in what is missing.
2. Draw a line under one word.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Read the timetable
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Use the timetable in Reading 3. Find each answer directly rather than reading the whole sheet.
1. What time does the Monday session start and finish?
2. Which room is the Saturday session in?
3. Which day is reading and writing?
4. When does the term begin?
5. Which week has no classes?

8. When is the exit test?
activities.answerSummary:
1. 18:00 to 20:00  2. Room 11  3. Wednesday  4. Monday 7 April  5. The week of 26 May  6. A notebook and a pen, and your enrolment card  7. More than four — so four is the limit  8. Saturday 28 June at 10:00

activities.title: Practice 5 — Which phrase?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
What would you say in each situation?
a) Somebody spoke and you caught nothing.
b) You heard every word but it went too fast.
c) There is one word you do not know.
d) You want to write down a word you have just heard.
e) You followed the start and lost the end.
f) You want to know if you may ask something.
What you say:
1. What does that word mean?
2. Can I ask a question?
3. Sorry, can you repeat that?
4. Sorry, I understood the first part but not the end.
5. How do you spell it?
6. Can you speak more slowly, please?
activities.answerSummary:
a-3 · b-6 · c-1 · d-5 · e-4 · f-2

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.sourceFile: Grade 1 Unit 1; Grade 2 Unit 1; Grade 3 Unit 2
activities.title: Practice 6 — Your own twenty minutes
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, keep a record. Each day, write one line: did you do your twenty minutes, where, and what did you do?
At the end of the week, count the days you managed.
Then answer two questions in writing: which day failed, and what was different about that day?
activities.answerSummary:
There is no key — this is about your week, not about English.
How to read your result: four or more days out of seven is working. Below four, the problem is almost never willpower, it is the slot. A slot that depends on something else happening first — after the children are asleep, when work is quiet — fails often. A slot attached to something that happens anyway — on the bus, while the water boils — survives.
If you managed fewer than four days, change the slot rather than trying harder, and record another week.

assignments.title: Ask four times, and plan your week
assignments.instructions: Two parts. Second, write your seven-day study plan from Writing 3, with a time, a place and one task for each day, and keep it. At the end of the week, tick the days you managed and add one sentence about what that tells you. Keep both together.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example before its practice and every exercise has its answer key. Pattern 3 and Practice 3 exist specifically so a learner working alone can read an unfamiliar instruction and act on it — the one skill a self-access course cannot do without. If you are running this with a group, the material below is an accelerator rather than a repair.

teacherNotes.noteType: The third-person s and why it survives
teacherNotes.note: This is the most common written error in beginner English and the least urgent to the learner, because dropping it costs no meaning at all. She like English is perfectly clear, so the conversation never applies pressure. Treat it as a proofreading habit rather than a comprehension problem: a learner who checks every verb after he, she or it at the end of a piece of writing will fix it faster than one who is corrected during speech.

teacherNotes.noteType: Pattern 4 is the highest-value five minutes in the level
teacherNotes.note: Learners who can interrupt politely get more practice from every conversation than learners who nod, and the gap compounds over months. Speaking 4 asks for ten repetitions of each phrase rather than five, deliberately — these have to arrive without assembly, at the moment when the learner is least able to construct anything.

teacherNotes.noteType: Reading 1 is a study-skills text, not a filler
teacherNotes.note: The twenty-minute argument is worth taking seriously with adults, who typically have very little time and blame themselves for it. Writing 3 turns it into a concrete plan attached to slots that already exist in the week, and Practice 6 tests it against a real week. Learners who fail Practice 6 have usually chosen a slot that depends on something else happening first — that is the thing to change, not their effort.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. She can speak three languages. (no to)
2. Can you help me? (no do — just move can to the front)
3. He can read but he cannot write. (no s on can)
4. I can come on Monday. (no to)
5. Can she repeat that? (no to)
Every one of these five is one of the three errors. If you got all five, this pattern is finished.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. reads  2. work  3. practises  4. like  5. speaks  6. study
Negatives: She does not read the news every morning. I do not like the speaking exercises.
Number 5 is the one to check — my teacher is one person, so it behaves exactly like he or she and takes the s. Watch the negatives too: once you use does, the s moves onto does and comes off the main verb.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Draw a line under the verb — one word in each sentence.
2. Join each word in one list to the right meaning in the other list.
3. Rearrange them so they are in the right sequence.
4. Fill in the empty boxes in the table.
5. Put a ✓ next to the right one — not a circle, not a line.
6. Find them in a dictionary.
If you were unsure about any of these, write it in your notebook. You will meet all six many times.

1. Sorry, can you repeat that?
2. Can you speak more slowly, please?
3. What does ____ mean?
4. How do you spell it?

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. reads  2. work  3. speaks  4. practise  5. studies  6. come  7. costs  8. likes  9. speak  10. write  11. does not like  12. understand
Four to look at. Number 3 and number 8 — my teacher and my neighbour are each one person, so they behave exactly like he or she. Number 5 — study becomes studies, because the y changes to ies. Numbers 11 and 12 — once does or do appears, the s moves onto it and comes off the main verb.
Ten or more correct means this is working. Below ten, redo the Pattern 2 card first.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
There is no key — this is about your week, not about English.
How to read your result: four or more days out of seven is working. Below four, the problem is almost never willpower, it is the slot. A slot that depends on something else happening first — after the children are asleep, when work is quiet — fails often. A slot attached to something that happens anyway — on the bus, while the water boils — survives.
If you managed fewer than four days, change the slot rather than trying harder, and record another week.
